# 12-Week Strength Programme: Post-Discectomy Desk Worker, 42M

## Programme Overview

This programme is built around your client's specific contraindications: no heavy spinal loading (so we'll avoid back squats, conventional deadlifts, barbell rows, overhead press with significant load) and no loaded spinal flexion (no Jefferson curls, weighted sit-ups, GHD sit-ups, or sloppy hip-hinge work under load). Instead, we'll lean on machines, unilateral work, supported variations, and neutral-spine patterns — all of which can still build excellent general strength.

The phases progress from **rebuilding capacity and motor control (weeks 1–4)**, into **hypertrophy and structural strength (weeks 5–8)**, and finishing with **strength expression and confidence (weeks 9–12)**. Sessions are 3x/week full-body, which suits a desk worker's recovery and schedule, with a daily "spine hygiene" mini-routine to counter sitting.

A typical session structure: 5-min bike or rower warm-up → core/spine prep → main lift → secondary lifts → accessories → finisher/conditioning.

---

## Phase 1: Foundation & Motor Control (Weeks 1–4)

**Goals:** Reintroduce load tolerance, groove hip-dominant and neutral-spine patterns, build trunk endurance (McGill-style), restore single-leg control.

**Loading:** RPE 6–7, leave 3–4 reps in reserve. We are building tissue tolerance, not chasing PRs.

### Weekly Session A — Lower Emphasis (Hip-Dominant)

- **Core prep:** McGill Big 3 — Curl-up 3×10s holds, Side plank 2×20s/side, Bird dog 3×8/side
- **Trap bar deadlift (high handles)** — 4×6 @ RPE 6. High handles reduce hip flexion demand and keep the spine more vertical than conventional pulls.
- **Goblet squat** — 3×8. Front-loaded so the torso stays upright; no spinal compression like a back squat.
- **Single-leg leg press** — 3×10/leg
- **Seated hamstring curl** — 3×12
- **Pallof press** — 3×10/side
- **Finish:** Dead bug 2×10/side

### Weekly Session B — Upper Emphasis

- **Core prep:** Same McGill Big 3
- **Chest-supported dumbbell row** — 4×8. Chest support eliminates spinal shear.
- **Landmine press (half-kneeling)** — 3×8/side. Easier on the spine than overhead barbell pressing.
- **Neutral-grip lat pulldown** — 3×10
- **Incline dumbbell press** — 3×10
- **Face pulls** — 3×15
- **Farmer's carry** — 3×30m (moderate load, focus on rib-down posture)

### Weekly Session C — Full Body / Single-Leg Focus

- **Core prep:** Bird dog 3×8/side, Side plank 2×30s/side
- **Rear-foot elevated split squat (dumbbells)** — 4×8/leg
- **Cable row (tall kneeling)** — 3×10
- **45° back extension (bodyweight, neutral spine, hip hinge only)** — 3×12. This is hip extension, NOT spinal flexion — coach it carefully.
- **Half-kneeling single-arm cable press** — 3×10/side
- **Suitcase carry** — 3×30m/side
- **Finish:** Side plank with reach 2×8/side

### Week-by-week progression (Phase 1)
- **Week 1:** As prescribed, RPE 6, focus on technique and breathing
- **Week 2:** Add ~5% load on main lifts, RPE 6–7
- **Week 3:** Add another set to main lift (e.g., 5×6), or +5% load
- **Week 4:** Deload — drop main lift sets by 30%, keep technique sharp; this gives connective tissue time to consolidate

---

## Phase 2: Hypertrophy & Structural Strength (Weeks 5–8)

**Goals:** Build muscle mass (especially glutes, lats, posterior chain), increase work capacity, progress loading on safe patterns.

**Loading:** RPE 7–8 on main work, RPE 8–9 on accessories. Rep ranges 6–12.

### Session A — Lower (Hip-Dominant)

- **Trunk prep:** Bird dog 2×8/side, Pallof press 2×10/side
- **Trap bar deadlift** — 4×5 @ RPE 7–8 (progress to RPE 8 by week 7)
- **Hip thrust (barbell, with bench pad)** — 4×8
- **Bulgarian split squat** — 3×8/leg, dumbbells
- **Lying hamstring curl** — 3×10
- **Standing calf raise** — 3×12
- **Cable woodchop (anti-rotation tempo)** — 3×10/side

### Session B — Upper Push/Pull

- **Trunk prep:** McGill Big 3, abbreviated
- **Chest-supported row** — 4×6 (progress load)
- **Incline dumbbell press** — 4×8
- **Neutral-grip pulldown** — 3×10
- **Landmine press** — 3×10/side
- **Dumbbell lateral raise** — 3×12
- **Rope triceps pushdown** — 3×12
- **EZ-bar curl (standing, ribs down)** — 3×10

### Session C — Lower (Quad-Dominant) / Carry

- **Trunk prep:** Side plank 2×30s/side, dead bug 2×10/side
- **Front-foot elevated reverse lunge** — 4×8/leg
- **Leg press** — 3×10 (moderate depth, don't let lumbar tuck)
- **Romanian deadlift, dumbbells** — 3×8 @ RPE 7 (strict neutral spine; if form breaks, sub for cable pull-through)
- **Cable pull-through** — 3×12
- **Heavy farmer's carry** — 4×30m
- **Hanging knee raise (no posterior tilt at top)** — 3×10

### Week-by-week progression (Phase 2)
- **Week 5:** Introduce new exercises at RPE 7, conservative loads
- **Week 6:** +5% on compounds, push accessories to RPE 8
- **Week 7:** Top-end: main lifts at RPE 8, accessories at RPE 9, add a rep or set
- **Week 8:** Deload — reduce volume by 40%, keep one heavyish single on main lift to maintain neural quality

---

## Phase 3: Strength Expression & Confidence (Weeks 9–12)

**Goals:** Demonstrate strength gains, increase load on key patterns within safe limits, build the client's confidence in his body. We don't need to test 1RMs — we'll express strength via heavier 3–5 rep work on lifts we trust.

**Loading:** RPE 7–9 on mains, working into heavier 3–5 rep ranges on safest patterns.

### Session A — Lower Strength

- **Trunk prep:** Big 3
- **Trap bar deadlift** — 5×3 @ RPE 8 (weeks 9–11)
- **Barbell hip thrust** — 4×6 @ RPE 8
- **Walking lunge, dumbbells** — 3×8/leg
- **Seated leg curl** — 3×10
- **Pallof press iso-hold** — 3×30s/side

### Session B — Upper Strength

- **Trunk prep:** Bird dog, side plank
- **Chest-supported row** — 5×5 @ RPE 8
- **Incline DB press** — 4×6
- **Half-kneeling landmine press** — 3×8/side
- **Weighted pull-up or neutral-grip pulldown** — 3×8
- **Rear delt fly** — 3×12
- **Hammer curl** — 3×10
- **Heavy farmer's carry** — 3×40m

### Session C — Lower Hybrid / Athletic

- **Trunk prep:** Big 3
- **Front-foot elevated split squat** — 4×6/leg, heavy DBs
- **Single-leg leg press** — 3×8/leg
- **Cable pull-through** — 3×10
- **Step-up, dumbbells** — 3×8/leg
- **Sled push or weighted carry medley** — 4 rounds
- **Side plank with leg lift** — 3×8/side

### Week-by-week progression (Phase 3)
- **Week 9:** Intro week to new rep scheme, RPE 7
- **Week 10:** +5% on main lifts, RPE 8
- **Week 11:** Heaviest week — RPE 8–9 on mains, AMRAP final set on the last set of the trap bar deadlift if technique is pristine
- **Week 12:** Taper week — reduce volume 50%, keep intensity moderate (RPE 7); finish on a high, fresh note. Optional retest of trap bar 3RM if client wants a tangible marker.

---

## Daily "Spine Hygiene" Routine (5–10 min, every day)

Counters his desk job and supports recovery:

- **Cat-cow** — 8 reps (gentle, pain-free range only — this is mobility, not loaded flexion)
- **Hip flexor stretch (couch stretch)** — 45s/side
- **90/90 hip switches** — 8/side
- **Glute bridge** — 10 reps
- **Bird dog** — 6/side
- **Dead hang from a bar** — 20–30s, 2 sets (decompression)

Encourage him to break up sitting every 30 minutes at work — even just standing and walking 60 seconds.

---

## Recovery & Lifestyle Notes

- **Sleep:** 7–8 hours non-negotiable. Disc tissue rehydrates overnight, and he should avoid heavy loading first thing in the morning (Adams & Hutton's research suggests waiting at least an hour after waking before significant spine loading).
- **Hydration:** 2.5–3 L/day — discs are largely water.
- **Walking:** 7,000–10,000 steps/day. This is the single best non-gym intervention for spine health in a desk worker.
- **Conditioning:** 1–2 low-impact cardio sessions/week (bike, rower with neutral spine, incline treadmill walk). Avoid running early on; can reintroduce in Phase 3 if pain-free.

---

## Red Flags — Stop and Reassess

Pause and reach out to his physio if he experiences: returning leg pain or numbness, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes after a session, sharp pain (not muscular soreness) during or after a lift, or any bowel/bladder changes (medical emergency).

## Lifts We're Deliberately Avoiding (and Why)

- **Back squat / front squat with significant load** — axial compression risk
- **Conventional barbell deadlift** — high shear forces and harder to maintain neutral lumbar at his current stage
- **Barbell bent-over row** — sustained loaded hip hinge with rotational/shear demand
- **Standing overhead press, heavy** — significant lumbar extension and compression
- **Sit-ups, crunches, GHD sit-ups, Jefferson curls** — loaded spinal flexion, directly contraindicated
- **Good mornings** — high lumbar shear

If he progresses excellently and remains symptom-free, some of these (e.g., goblet front squat → eventually a safety bar squat, or rack pulls from above knee) can be reintroduced in a subsequent block — but I'd want a physio sign-off before that conversation.

Let me know if you'd like me to swap exercises based on his gym's equipment, build out the conditioning side in more detail, or add a nutrition component.

# Nutrition Component: Anti-Inflammatory Eating

This sits alongside the 12-week strength programme. The aim isn't a restrictive "diet" — it's a sustainable shift in eating patterns that supports disc and joint health, training recovery, body composition (most desk workers carry some excess adiposity that increases systemic inflammation), and long-term spine resilience. We'll structure it as principles, a daily template, a weekly plan, and supplement guidance.

---

## Why Anti-Inflammatory Eating Matters for This Client

Chronic low-grade inflammation is implicated in disc degeneration, slower tissue repair, and persistent pain sensitisation. For a 42-year-old desk worker recovering from a disc herniation, the goals are:

1. **Reduce systemic inflammatory load** (lower omega-6:omega-3 ratio, reduce ultra-processed food, manage blood glucose)
2. **Support connective tissue repair** (adequate protein, collagen precursors, vitamin C, zinc)
3. **Maintain or modestly reduce body fat** — every kilo of excess weight is extra load on the lumbar spine and pro-inflammatory adipose tissue
4. **Optimise recovery** so he can train hard within his restrictions

---

## Core Principles

### 1. Build every meal around a protein source
Target **1.6–2.0 g protein per kg bodyweight per day**, spread across 3–4 meals. Protein supports muscle repair (he's a 42-year-old, so anabolic resistance is starting to matter) and connective tissue turnover. Prioritise:
- Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout) — 2–3 portions/week minimum
- Eggs
- Poultry, lean red meat (2–3x/week max for red meat)
- Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese
- Legumes, tofu, tempeh

### 2. Half the plate as colour
Aim for **6–8 portions of vegetables and fruit per day**, emphasising variety and colour. Polyphenols and flavonoids are where the real anti-inflammatory action lives.
- **Daily non-negotiables:** a handful of berries, a portion of leafy greens, a portion of cruciferous veg (broccoli, cabbage, rocket)
- **Rotate in:** beetroot, peppers, tomatoes (cooked is better for lycopene), carrots, sweet potato, courgette

### 3. Fats: prioritise omega-3, monounsaturated, and reduce omega-6
- **Increase:** oily fish, walnuts, flaxseed (ground), chia seeds, extra virgin olive oil, avocado
- **Reduce:** sunflower/corn/vegetable oils, deep-fried foods, ultra-processed snacks
- **Cooking fat:** extra virgin olive oil for low-medium heat, butter or avocado oil for higher heat

### 4. Carbs: smart choices, not low-carb
He's training hard — he needs carbs. The aim is to swap refined carbs for whole-food carbs:
- **Yes:** oats, quinoa, brown rice, sweet potato, regular potato (with skin), wholegrain sourdough, beans, lentils, fruit
- **Limit:** white bread, pastries, sugary drinks, breakfast cereals, biscuits

### 5. Spice the food
Several culinary herbs/spices have meaningful anti-inflammatory effects. Use generously:
- **Turmeric** (with black pepper to boost absorption)
- **Ginger** (fresh in stir-fries, tea, smoothies)
- **Garlic** (raw or lightly cooked)
- **Cinnamon** (porridge, yoghurt)
- **Rosemary, thyme, oregano**

### 6. Hydration & alcohol
- **Water:** 2.5–3 L/day (also supports disc hydration)
- **Coffee/green tea:** both contain anti-inflammatory polyphenols — fine, even beneficial. Cap caffeine by 2pm.
- **Alcohol:** ideally ≤4 units/week. Alcohol is pro-inflammatory, disrupts sleep (key for disc recovery), and stalls fat loss.

### 7. Minimise the inflammatory drivers
- Ultra-processed foods (anything with a long ingredient list of things you wouldn't have in your kitchen)
- Added sugars (target <30g/day)
- Processed meats (bacon, salami, sausages — fine occasionally, not daily)
- Industrial seed oils
- Sugary drinks and fruit juice

- **Vitamin D3:** 1,000–2,000 IU/day, especially Oct–April in the UK. Low vit D is associated with chronic pain and poor musculoskeletal recovery. Ideally test levels first.

- **Collagen peptides:** 15 g taken ~60 min before training, with vitamin C. Emerging evidence for connective tissue, particularly tendon and possibly disc/cartilage.
- **Magnesium glycinate:** 200–400 mg in the evening if sleep is poor or he gets muscle cramps.

- Multivitamins (low yield if diet is good)
- BCAAs (redundant if protein intake is adequate)
- Glucosamine/chondroitin (weak evidence for spinal discs)
- Greens powders (expensive, real vegetables are better)

# Cardio Addition: 2x/Week

Slotting cardio in alongside three strength sessions is very doable for a 42-year-old desk worker — in fact, it's almost essential. Cardiovascular work supports disc health (improved nutrient diffusion to avascular disc tissue), reduces systemic inflammation, aids recovery between strength sessions, and addresses the cardiometabolic risk that comes with desk work.

We'll structure cardio as **one low-intensity steady-state (LISS) session** and **one moderate interval session**, both selected to avoid spinal loading and impact. The format progresses across the three phases alongside the strength programme.

---

## Weekly Schedule

The ideal layout, assuming strength sessions Mon/Wed/Fri:

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Strength A |
| Tue | **Cardio 1 — LISS** |
| Wed | Strength B |
| Thu | Rest / spine hygiene + walking |
| Fri | Strength C |
| Sat | **Cardio 2 — Intervals** |
| Sun | Rest / walking |

**Key rule:** never schedule cardio the day before a heavy lower body strength session in Phase 3. If the week shifts, prioritise putting cardio on a non-strength day or after a strength session, not before.

---

## Modality Selection

We're filtering out anything that's high-impact or compresses/flexes the spine repetitively. **Good options:**

- **Stationary bike (upright or recumbent)** — recumbent is ideal early on; upright once he's tolerating well
- **Rower** — *only if* he can maintain neutral spine and hip-hinge cleanly; otherwise defer until Phase 2
- **Elliptical / cross-trainer** — excellent low-impact option
- **Incline treadmill walking** — superb, no impact, big calorie burn
- **Swimming** — freestyle or backstroke; avoid breaststroke (lumbar extension)
- **Ski erg** — great upper-body bias, low spinal load
- **Sled push/drag** — counts as interval cardio in Phase 3

**Avoid initially:** running, jumping, plyometrics, spin classes with poor positioning, breaststroke.

---

## Phase 1: Build Aerobic Base (Weeks 1–4)

**Goal:** Re-establish cardiovascular fitness gently, build the habit, avoid any aggravation.

### Cardio 1 — LISS (Tuesday)
- **Modality:** Recumbent bike or incline treadmill walk
- **Duration:** 25–35 min
- **Intensity:** Zone 2 — conversational pace, RPE 4–5, can hold a full conversation, nose-breathing possible
- **HR target:** roughly 60–70% of max HR (~108–125 bpm for a 42-year-old)

### Cardio 2 — Easy Intervals (Saturday)
- **Modality:** Bike or elliptical
- **Format:** 5 min warm-up → **6 rounds of (1 min moderate / 2 min easy)** → 5 min cool-down
- **Total:** ~28 min
- **Intensity:** "Moderate" = RPE 6, slightly breathy but in control. We are *not* going hard yet.

### Week-by-week
- **Week 1:** LISS 25 min; Intervals 5 rounds
- **Week 2:** LISS 30 min; Intervals 6 rounds
- **Week 3:** LISS 35 min; Intervals 7 rounds
- **Week 4 (deload):** LISS 25 min easy; skip intervals, do a 30-min walk outside instead

---

## Phase 2: Build Capacity (Weeks 5–8)

**Goal:** Increase aerobic volume and introduce slightly harder intervals. He's tolerating loading well by now, so we can push the engine a bit.

### Cardio 1 — LISS (Tuesday)
- **Modality:** Incline treadmill walk, bike, or swim
- **Duration:** 35–45 min
- **Intensity:** Zone 2, RPE 4–5
- **Optional:** alternate between incline walk and swim week to week for variety and joint relief

### Cardio 2 — Intervals (Saturday)
- **Modality:** Bike, rower (if form is solid), or elliptical
- **Format:** 5 min warm-up → **8 rounds of (1 min hard / 90 sec easy)** → 5 min cool-down
- **Total:** ~30 min
- **Intensity:** "Hard" = RPE 7–8, breathing heavily but not all-out. Cannot speak in full sentences during work intervals.

### Week-by-week
- **Week 5:** LISS 35 min; Intervals 6 rounds
- **Week 6:** LISS 40 min; Intervals 7 rounds
- **Week 7:** LISS 45 min; Intervals 8 rounds
- **Week 8 (deload):** LISS 30 min easy; replace intervals with an easy outdoor walk or swim

---

## Phase 3: Performance & Variety (Weeks 9–12)

**Goal:** Maintain aerobic base while introducing higher-intensity work and an athletic finisher option (sled). Cardio volume comes down slightly so strength can peak.

### Cardio 1 — LISS (Tuesday)
- **Modality:** His choice — pick what he enjoys most so it sticks long-term
- **Duration:** 40 min
- **Intensity:** Zone 2

### Cardio 2 — Mixed Intervals (Saturday)
Choose **one** of the following formats each week (rotate for variety):

**Option A — Bike VO2 intervals**
5 min warm-up → **5 rounds of (2 min hard / 2 min easy)** → 5 min cool-down. RPE 8 on work.

**Option B — Sled medley** (great athletic option, zero spinal compression)
5 min warm-up → **8 rounds of (30m sled push / 30m sled drag / 60s rest)** → easy walk to cool down.

**Option C — Rower or ski erg intervals**
5 min warm-up → **10 rounds of (250m hard / 90 sec rest)** → 5 min cool-down.

### Week-by-week
- **Week 9:** LISS 40 min; Intervals Option A
- **Week 10:** LISS 40 min; Intervals Option B
- **Week 11:** LISS 35 min; Intervals Option C (heaviest training week — keep cardio in check)
- **Week 12 (taper):** LISS 30 min easy; skip intervals, do a 45-min easy bike ride or outdoor walk for enjoyment

- Energy holding up across the week
- Strength sessions still feel strong (especially Friday)
- Resting HR stable or trending down
- Sleep good

**Signs to dial it back:**
- Strength performance dropping
- Persistent fatigue or low mood
- Resting HR creeping up >5 bpm over baseline
- Any return of low back symptoms

If any of those show up, cut interval volume in half first and keep LISS — LISS is restorative, intervals are stressful.

- **Total daily intake:** if he's targeting fat loss in Phase 2, the added cardio (~400–500 kcal/week of expenditure) gives a little extra room without needing to cut food further. Don't stack a steep deficit *and* added cardio — recovery suffers and so does the back.

# Safe Abs Work for a Post-Discectomy Client

Good news: he can absolutely train his abs hard and get visible, strong results. We just need to pick exercises that build the trunk **without loaded spinal flexion** (the exact mechanism that herniates discs). The framework here is from Stuart McGill's work on spine biomechanics — train the trunk for what it's actually for: **resisting movement, not creating it.**

---

## The Four Categories of Safe Trunk Training

Effective, spine-safe abs work falls into four buckets. Programme across all four for complete development:

1. **Anti-extension** — resisting the spine arching backward (planks, dead bugs, rollouts)
2. **Anti-rotation** — resisting twisting forces (Pallof press, half-kneeling chops)
3. **Anti-lateral flexion** — resisting sideways bending (side planks, suitcase carries)
4. **Hip flexion with neutral spine** — training the rectus abdominis and hip flexors *without* rounding the lumbar (hanging leg raises done correctly, reverse crunches with no posterior pelvic tilt)

This covers everything the abs are anatomically designed to do.

---

## What He Should Avoid

To be explicit, so there's no ambiguity:

- ❌ Crunches and sit-ups
- ❌ Weighted decline sit-ups
- ❌ GHD sit-ups
- ❌ Jefferson curls
- ❌ Russian twists with rotation through the lumbar spine
- ❌ Toes-to-bar (the dynamic version with lumbar flexion at the top)
- ❌ Cable crunches (loaded spinal flexion — one of the worst offenders)
- ❌ V-ups
- ❌ Ab wheel rollout *if* he can't keep a neutral spine throughout (most people can't initially — see progression below)

---

## The Exercise Menu

### Anti-Extension (the main "abs burn" category)

**Beginner / Phase 1:**
- **Dead bug** — 3×8/side, slow and controlled, ribs glued to the floor
- **Hollow body hold (knees bent)** — 3×20–30s
- **Front plank** — 3×30–45s, with active "ribs down, glutes squeezed" cue

**Intermediate / Phase 2:**
- **Long-lever dead bug** (straighter legs) — 3×8/side
- **Hollow body hold (legs straight)** — 3×20–30s
- **RKC plank** (max tension plank) — 3×15–20s — this is brutal, in a good way
- **Stir the pot** (forearms on Swiss ball, small circles) — 3×8 each direction

**Advanced / Phase 3:**
- **Ab wheel rollout from knees** — 3×6–8, *only if* he can maintain neutral spine throughout. Coach: ribs down, glutes squeezed, "push the floor away." Stop short of any lumbar extension.
- **Body saw** (forearms on sliders, push body back and forward) — 3×8
- **TRX fallout** — 3×8–10

### Anti-Rotation

**Beginner / Phase 1:**
- **Pallof press** (cable or band, half-kneeling or tall kneeling) — 3×10/side
- **Pallof iso-hold** — 3×20s/side

**Intermediate / Phase 2:**
- **Tall-kneeling cable chop** (anti-rotation tempo — slow, controlled, no spinal twist) — 3×10/side
- **Pallof press with overhead reach** — 3×8/side
- **Bird dog with band resistance** — 3×6/side

**Advanced / Phase 3:**
- **Half-kneeling cable chop and lift** — 3×8/side
- **Landmine rainbow** (controlled, hips do the work, spine stays neutral) — 3×6/side
- **Renegade row** (light dumbbells, no hip sway) — 3×6/side

### Anti-Lateral Flexion

**Beginner / Phase 1:**
- **Side plank from knees** — 3×20–30s/side
- **Suitcase carry** (already in his programme) — 3×30m/side

**Intermediate / Phase 2:**
- **Full side plank** — 3×30–45s/side
- **Side plank with top leg lift** — 3×8/side
- **Heavy suitcase carry** — 3×30m/side

**Advanced / Phase 3:**
- **Copenhagen plank** (top leg on bench, advanced adductor/oblique work) — 3×15–25s/side
- **Side plank with row** (cable) — 3×8/side
- **Single-arm overhead carry** — 3×20m/side

### Hip Flexion with Neutral Spine

This is where he can train the "six-pack look" safely:

**Beginner / Phase 1:**
- **Reverse crunch with NO posterior pelvic tilt at the top** — knees come toward chest, but the lower back stays in contact with the floor and doesn't curl. 3×10. Most people do this wrong; coach carefully.
- **Standing march** with band around feet — 3×10/side

**Intermediate / Phase 2:**
- **Hanging knee raise** (knees come up to hip height, no pelvic tilt at the top, no swinging) — 3×8–10
- **Captain's chair knee raise** — 3×10

**Advanced / Phase 3:**
- **Hanging straight-leg raise** (straight legs to horizontal, no lumbar movement, no kipping) — 3×6–8
- **L-sit holds** on parallettes or rings — 3×10–20s
- **Toes-to-rings with controlled negative**, *only* if pelvis stays neutral — 3×5

---

## Programming Into His Week

His current programme already includes excellent trunk work (McGill Big 3, Pallof, carries, dead bugs). To make abs a more prominent focus without overhauling the plan, layer in **two dedicated abs blocks per week** as finishers — 8–10 minutes at the end of two strength sessions.

### Suggested layout

**End of Session A (Lower) — Anti-rotation + anti-lateral focus:**
- Pallof press — 3×10/side
- Side plank variation — 3×30s/side
- Suitcase carry — already in programme

**End of Session B (Upper) — Anti-extension + hip flexion focus:**
- Dead bug or hollow hold — 3 sets
- Hanging knee raise (or reverse crunch in Phase 1) — 3×8–10
- Plank variation — 2 sets

**Session C** keeps the existing trunk work (bird dog, side plank with reach) — don't add more, the carries already hit hard.

### Phase progression
- **Phase 1:** Beginner variations from each category. Focus is *quality of bracing* — teaching him to find and maintain neutral spine under tension.
- **Phase 2:** Move to intermediate variations. Add load to carries, increase plank time.
- **Phase 3:** Introduce advanced variations *if* technique is excellent. Hanging leg raises and ab wheel rollouts are the big graduation lifts.

---

## Coaching Cues That Matter

These three cues prevent 90% of problems:

1. **"Ribs down to hips"** — closes the rib cage, prevents lumbar extension, finds the canister position
2. **"Brace like you're about to be punched"** — 360° abdominal tension, not just sucking in
3. **"Spine stays a steel rod"** — particularly on rollouts, leg raises, and chops. Movement happens at the hips and shoulders, not the spine.

For the hanging leg raise specifically: cue him to **posteriorly tilt the pelvis *first*** (tuck the tailbone) before lifting the legs. This locks the lumbar spine in a safe position. If he kicks his legs up first, he'll arch his back to compensate.

## A Word on Aesthetics

He'll get visible abs faster from nutrition (already covered) than from any ab exercise. The training above builds **strong, thick, functional abs** that show through when body fat drops. Combined with the anti-inflammatory protocol in a modest deficit during Phase 2, he should see meaningful change in the mirror by week 8–12.

Good — if he's responding well and his back is quiet, we use that window. ## What's Changing

- **RPE on main lifts:** 8 (was 7–8), with one top set per week pushed to RPE 8.5
- **RPE on accessories:** 9, with the occasional AMRAP final set
- **Rep ranges:** dropping main lifts into 4–6 reps for a stronger neural stimulus
- **New variations:** safety bar squat (introduced cautiously), heavier hip thrusts, weighted carries, weighted pull-ups
- **Volume:** one extra set on key lifts; total session volume creeps up ~15%
- **Density:** tighter rest periods on accessories (60–75s) to drive metabolic stress

The frame still progresses: introduce → consolidate → push → deload.

## Session A — Lower (Hip-Dominant), Intensity Push

- **Trunk prep:** Bird dog 2×8/side, Pallof press 2×10/side
- **Trap bar deadlift (high handles)** — **5×4 @ RPE 8**, top set to RPE 8.5 by week 7

- **Safety bar squat** (introduced week 5, *only if* tolerated — see notes below) — 3×6 @ RPE 7

The safety bar squat is the call here, not the back squat. The yoke and front handles keep the torso more upright than a back squat and load the spine less aggressively, but it's still axial loading. ## Week-by-Week Progression

- **Week 5 (introduction):** New variations introduced at conservative loads, RPE 7–8. Goal is to learn the exercises (especially SSB squat and weighted pull-up) and confirm tolerance.
- **Week 6 (consolidation):** Same lifts, +5% load on mains, accessories pushed to RPE 8–9. Volume holds.
- **Week 7 (push):** Top set of trap bar deadlift to RPE 8.5. Add one set to hip thrust and chest-supported row. AMRAP final set on Bulgarian split squats and weighted pull-ups.
- **Week 8 (deload):** Drop volume 40%, drop intensity to RPE 6–7. One quality set of each main lift at moderate weight, accessories at 50% volume. Non-negotiable — the deload is where adaptation lands.

## Cardio Adjustment for the Push

Don't stack cardio intensity on top of strength intensity. Pull the intervals back slightly so recovery doesn't get compromised:

- **Tuesday LISS:** unchanged — 35–45 min Zone 2
- **Saturday Intervals:** drop to **6 rounds** of (1 min hard / 90s easy) across weeks 5–7. Skip intervals entirely in week 8 — replace with a 40-min easy walk or swim.

## Nutrition Adjustment for the Push

Heavier loading needs more fuel. A few tweaks:

- **Protein:** push to the upper end — **2.0 g/kg/day** for the duration of Phase 2
- **Carbs:** add 30–50g carbs on strength training days (extra portion of rice, oats, or potato — preferably around the session)

- **Sleep:** the variable that matters most. Heavier training without 7.5+ hours of sleep is a fast track to nothing working. Worth explicitly checking in on.

## Monitoring — When to Pull Back

Push intensity is great until it isn't. Specific red/amber flags for this client:

**Pull back immediately if:**
- Any return of leg symptoms (numbness, tingling, radiating pain)
- Morning back stiffness lasting >30 minutes
- Sharp pain (not muscular soreness) during or after a lift
- Strength performance regressing two sessions in a row

**Amber flags — reduce intensity 10–15%:**
- Resting HR up >5 bpm over baseline for 3+ days
- Sleep quality dropping
- Persistent low mood or motivation drop
- Joint achiness (knees, hips) creeping in

If everything's quiet, you finish Phase 2 with him meaningfully stronger and ready for the heavier 3–5 rep ranges in Phase 3. If the back gets noisy at any point, revert to the original Phase 2 prescription and don't push it — there's no PR worth a re-herniation.

# Building in a 1RM Test — Week 12

Reasonable request, and the trap bar deadlift (high handles) is the right lift for it. It's the heaviest, most spine-friendly compound in his programme — high handles reduce hip flexion, the neutral grip keeps the load close to the centre of mass, and there's no axial compression on a loaded bar across the back.

A few things to be clear about up front:

- **One lift only.** We're testing the trap bar deadlift. Not multiple lifts in a session, not a "powerlifting total." One quality expression of strength.
- **Pristine technique is the gate.** If form breaks down on the warm-up sets, we cap the test and call it. He doesn't *need* a number — he wants a number. We protect the back.
- **High handles, neutral spine, controlled.** This is not a max-effort grinder. If a rep looks ugly, it's the last rep.
- **Physio clearance.** Worth a quick check-in with his physio before week 12 if he hasn't been recently. Documents the milestone and covers everyone.

The plan below restructures Phase 3 slightly to build into the test rather than just bolt it on.

---

## Restructured Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12) for a 1RM Peak

The original Phase 3 was already a strength expression block, so the shape doesn't change radically — we just sharpen the peaking week and taper properly.

### Week 9 — Intro
As originally programmed. Trap bar deadlift **5×3 @ RPE 7**, RPE-capped working sets, focus on bar speed.

### Week 10 — Build
Trap bar deadlift **4×3 @ RPE 8**. Drop the 5th set — quality over volume. After working sets, do **one heavy single at RPE 8** (around 85% of estimated max) to start grooving heavier loads. This is rehearsal, not a test.

### Week 11 — Heavy Single
Trap bar deadlift **work up to a heavy single at RPE 8.5** (~90% of estimated max). Followed by **2×3 backoff @ 80%**. This is the dress rehearsal. The single he hits here gives us a reliable opener for week 12.

Also in week 11: reduce hip thrust and Bulgarian split squat volume by one set each to leave him fresh for the deload.

### Week 12 — Taper & Test

**Mon (Session A — heavy day reduced to a primer):**
- Trunk prep, abbreviated
- Trap bar deadlift — work up to **a single at RPE 7** (around 80% of expected max). Crisp, fast, ribs locked. No grinding. Done.
- Hip thrust — 2×6 @ RPE 6
- Pallof iso-hold — 2×30s/side
- Done. Out of the gym in 35 min.

**Tue:** LISS cardio, 25 min easy

**Wed (Session B — upper, light):**
- Chest-supported row — 3×6 @ RPE 6
- Incline DB press — 3×6 @ RPE 6
- Neutral-grip pulldown — 3×8
- Face pulls — 2×15
- 30 min, done.

**Thu:** Full rest, walking only. Hydration, sleep, food on point.

## Test Day Protocol — Trap Bar Deadlift 1RM

### Before the session

- **Sleep:** 8 hours minimum the two nights prior
- **Food:** normal breakfast 2–3 hours before, no novel foods, moderate carbs, light on fat and fibre
- **Caffeine:** 200–300mg ~45 min before warm-up if he tolerates it well (don't experiment on test day)
- **Hydration:** sipped consistently through the morning, not chugged at the last minute
- **Arrival:** at least 20 min before he plans to start warming up — no rushing

### Pre-test warm-up (15–20 min)

- 5 min bike, easy
- McGill Big 3: curl-up 2×10s, side plank 2×20s/side, bird dog 2×8/side
- Hip flexor stretch 30s/side
- 90/90 hip switches 6/side
- Glute bridge 10 reps
- Bodyweight squats 10 reps
- Pallof press 2×8/side
- Two empty trap bar warm-ups: 10 reps slow, 5 reps with bar speed intent

### Warm-up sets

Assuming an estimated 1RM of **180 kg** (adjust the numbers — these are illustrative percentages of his actual estimated max). Rest 2–3 min between warm-ups, 3–5 min between top attempts.

| Set | % of est. 1RM | Reps | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 40% | 5 | Groove the pattern |
| 2 | 55% | 5 | Bar speed should be snappy |
| 3 | 70% | 3 | First heavy feel |
| 4 | 80% | 2 | Sharp, controlled |
| 5 | 87% | 1 | Last rehearsal rep |
| **Opener** | **92%** | **1** | First real attempt — should move well, RPE 8 |
| **Second** | **97%** | **1** | RPE 9, this matches week 11's heavy single |
| **Third (PR attempt)** | **100–103%** | **1** | Only if the second moved well |

### Rules during the test

1. **Three attempts maximum.** No fourth attempts. If he misses the third, the second was the lift.
2. **Form gate:** if his rounded back posture shows on a warm-up at 80% or above, the test ends with the last clean lift. No negotiation.
3. **No grinding reps.** If the bar slows to a halt mid-pull or his hips shoot up disproportionately, drop it. A clean RPE 9 single is a far better outcome than a ground-out, technique-broken 1RM.
4. **Belt:** allowed for top three sets only. He should have been using it on heavier sets through Phase 3 so it's not novel.
5. **Straps:** allowed if grip is the limiting factor — we're testing leg/hip strength, not grip.
6. **Reset between reps and between attempts.** Full reset on the floor, re-brace, re-grip.
7. **Coach the brace:** "big breath into the belt, ribs down, lats tight, push the floor away."

### After the test

- Cool down: 5 min easy bike, foam roll lats/glutes/quads
- Refuel: protein + carbs within 60 min
- Decompression hang from a bar: 2×20s
- Walk in the afternoon, easy
- Log the number, photo or video the top lift

---

## What to Test Instead of Adding More Lifts

He'll be tempted to ask "what about hip thrust 1RM? Bench? Pull-up max?" The answer is no — not in the same session, not in the same week. If he wants more markers to celebrate, capture these as **submaximal tests** during the test session warm-up day or the previous week:

- **Chest-supported row 5RM** (week 11)
- **Bulgarian split squat 6RM/leg** (week 11)
- **Max strict pull-ups** (week 11)
- **Heavy farmer's carry distance with a fixed load** (week 11)

These give him a full picture of his strength progress without stacking spinal risk.

---

## Contingency Plans

**If he wakes up on test day feeling off** (poor sleep, niggly back, low energy):
- Push the test to Sunday or Monday. The block isn't ruined by a 1–2 day shift. Far better to test fresh.

**If a warm-up set feels heavier than expected** (e.g., 80% feels like 90%):
- Lower the opener by 5%, lower the projected top by 5%, prioritise a clean PR over an ambitious miss.

**If the back gives any warning sign** during warm-ups (tightness, twinge, asymmetry):
- Call it. End the session with the last clean set. Tell him this is non-negotiable and agree it in advance, not in the moment.

**If he smashes the second attempt with bar speed to spare:**
- Third attempt at 102–103%, not higher. Big jumps on max attempts are how injuries happen.

## Setting Expectations With Him Now

Worth having a direct conversation in week 9 or 10. Something like:

> "We're going to test trap bar deadlift in week 12. The rules are: one lift, three attempts, technique is the gate. If your back gives any warning, we stop — and that's not a failure, that's the programme working. You'll get a real number you can be proud of, and we'll have a clean baseline to build the next block from."

Frames the test as a celebration of the work, not a high-stakes performance. Reduces the chance he tries to be a hero on a bad rep.

# Sleep & Recovery Protocol

Recovery is where the programme actually works. For a 42-year-old desk worker with a disc history pushing intensity in Phase 2 and peaking for a 1RM in week 12, sleep isn't optional — it's the variable that determines whether the work lands. Disc tissue rehydrates overnight, muscle protein synthesis peaks during deep sleep, and pain perception is meaningfully amplified by sleep deprivation. If he sleeps 6 hours he's a different client than if he sleeps 8.

This protocol covers sleep, daily recovery practices, weekly structured recovery, and how to flex it across the three phases.

---

## Sleep: The Non-Negotiables

### Targets
- **Duration:** 7.5–8.5 hours in bed, aiming for ~7.5 hours of actual sleep
- **Consistency:** same bedtime and wake time within a 30-minute window, including weekends
- **Quality marker:** waking without an alarm most days, alert within 15 min of waking

### The wind-down (90 min before bed)

This is the highest-leverage habit change for a desk worker. Most men in their 40s don't sleep badly because of their mattress — they sleep badly because they go from screens to pillow with no transition.

**T-90 min:**
- Last meal finished (or at least nothing heavy after this point)
- Dim the lights in the house — overhead lights off, lamps on
- Phone goes into another room or on greyscale + do-not-disturb

**T-60 min:**
- No more work, no more emails
- Hot shower or 10-min warm bath (the post-shower temperature drop is a strong sleep signal)
- Light reading, conversation, or stretching only

**T-30 min:**
- Bedroom prep: cool (17–19°C), dark (blackout if possible, eye mask if not), quiet (earplugs or white noise if needed)
- 5 min of spine hygiene (see daily routine — dead hang, cat-cow, hip flexor stretch)
- Box breathing or 4-7-8 breathing for 3–5 min in bed if his mind is busy

### Things to specifically remove

- **Phone in the bedroom** — single biggest fix. Get an alarm clock.
- **Alcohol in the 3 hours before bed** — it knocks him out but destroys deep sleep architecture. One pint with dinner is fine; two pints at 10pm is not.
- **Caffeine after 2pm** — half-life is ~6 hours. Coffee at 4pm is still working at 10pm.
- **Heavy/late training** — if he can't train before 7pm, he can, but he needs to extend the wind-down and avoid CNS-intense sessions late (interval cardio, heavy strength work)
- **Late large meals** — finish dinner 3 hours before bed where possible. Reflux + supine + disc-recovering spine is a bad combination.

### Morning anchor

The wake-up time is what sets the rhythm. Bedtime drifts because wake time drifts. Lock the wake time first.

- Same wake time daily (±30 min)
- **10 minutes of daylight within 30 min of waking** — outside, no sunglasses. This is the single strongest circadian signal we have. On dark winter mornings, a 10,000 lux light therapy lamp during breakfast does the same job.
- Coffee 60–90 min after waking, not immediately (lets adenosine clear naturally, reduces afternoon crash)
- Avoid heavy spinal loading in the **first 60 min after waking** — disc pressure is at its daily peak from overnight rehydration (Adams & Hutton). No deadlifts at 6am. If he must train early, extend the warm-up significantly and start lighter.

---

## Daily Recovery Practices

### Movement throughout the day

For a desk worker, this matters more than any single recovery modality:

- **Break sitting every 30 minutes** — 60-second stand, walk, or stretch. Set a timer.
- **Walking total:** 7,000–10,000 steps/day, ideally including a 15–20 min walk after lunch (helps glucose, mood, and spine)
- **Daily spine hygiene routine** (already in the programme — cat-cow, couch stretch, 90/90 switches, glute bridge, bird dog, dead hang)

### Hydration

- **Water:** 2.5–3 L/day, paced through the day (not all at once)
- **Electrolytes** on training days, especially Phase 3 (a pinch of salt + lemon in water, or a low-sugar electrolyte tab)
- Front-load fluids — most of the daily intake before 7pm to avoid night-time wake-ups

### Nutrition timing for recovery

- **Protein at every meal** (already covered) — distribution matters as much as total
- **Carbs post-training** — supports glycogen replenishment and improves sleep quality the same night
- **A small protein snack before bed** if dinner is early — Greek yoghurt or cottage cheese provides slow-release protein overnight (~20–30g). Useful in Phase 2 and Phase 3.
- **Tart cherry juice** — 30ml concentrate in the evening has some evidence for sleep quality and recovery; cheap experiment

### Stress management

Sympathetic dominance from work stress blunts recovery as much as physical training stress. Two simple anchors:

- **3–5 min of slow breathing** at lunch and before bed (box breathing: 4 in, 4 hold, 4 out, 4 hold)
- **One "off" evening per week** with no screens after 8pm — proper downshift

---

## Weekly Structured Recovery

Beyond daily habits, build in structured recovery sessions.

### Sunday — the recovery anchor day

- 30–60 min outdoor walk, ideally with daylight in the morning
- Optional sauna 15–20 min if access (good evidence for cardiovascular and recovery benefits in middle-aged men)
- Optional swim or sauna + cold shower contrast (2–3 rounds: 2 min warm, 30s cool)
- Full spine hygiene routine, slower and longer than usual (15 min)
- Earlier bedtime (Sunday is the foundation for the week — protect it)

### Mid-week downshift — Thursday

Already a rest day in the schedule. Treat it intentionally:
- No structured exercise
- 20–30 min easy walk
- Spine hygiene routine
- Earlier bedtime ideally — sets up Friday's strength session

### Mobility session — Saturday afternoon (optional)

15–20 min after the Saturday cardio:
- Couch stretch — 60s/side
- 90/90 hip switches — 8/side
- Pigeon stretch — 60s/side
- Thoracic spine opener (foam roller across upper back) — 90s
- Lat stretch (kneeling, hands on bench) — 45s/side
- Dead hang — 2×30s

---

## Phase-by-Phase Adjustments

### Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4) — Build the habit

The training load is moderate, so the focus is **installing the routines**. By the end of week 4 he should have:
- A consistent bedtime (within 30 min) for at least 5 nights/week
- Phone out of the bedroom
- Daily morning daylight habit
- Spine hygiene routine done daily

Don't add complexity. Just lock the basics.

### Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8) — Protect the push

Heavier training means recovery becomes more demanding:
- **Sleep target tightens:** 8 hours in bed, no flexibility on weeknights before training days
- **Add the pre-bed protein snack** on training days
- **Sunday sauna** introduced if available
- **Thursday becomes sacred** — no late nights Thursday during Phase 2

If sleep slips for more than 2 nights in a row during this phase, pull training intensity back 10–15% for the next session. Don't grind through.

### Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12) — Peaking recovery

This is where recovery quality determines whether the 1RM goes well:
- **Sleep priority absolute** — anything compromising sleep gets cut (late socialising, evening screens, late caffeine, late training)
- **Wind-down extends to 2 hours** in weeks 11–12
- **Alcohol reduced to zero** in week 11 and the start of week 12 (can resume after the test, in moderation)
- **Sauna/contrast** twice weekly if available
- **Extra sleep hour** the two nights before the 1RM test if achievable — go to bed an hour earlier, not wake an hour later

### Week 12 specifically

- **Monday–Wednesday:** all normal recovery practices, extra attention to sleep
- **Thursday:** full rest, no caffeine after noon, in bed by 10:30pm
- **Friday:** complete rest day, no alcohol, light dinner with carbs, in bed by 10pm, 8.5 hours minimum
- **Saturday morning (test day):** wake naturally if possible, daylight within 30 min, normal breakfast 2–3 hours pre-test, caffeine 45 min pre-warm-up

---

## Recovery Monitoring

Simple, low-burden, useful. Pick two or three of these, not all of them:

### Subjective (do these — they're more useful than wearables)

A morning 1–10 score on:
- **Sleep quality** (how rested do I feel?)
- **Energy** (motivation to train today)
- **Soreness** (general, not specific pain)
- **Back feel** (specific to him — any stiffness, twinges, tightness)

Log in a notes app, takes 30 seconds. Review weekly with him.

### Objective (optional)

- **Resting heart rate** — easiest marker. Trend matters more than daily reading. Up >5 bpm over 3-day baseline = recovery is compromised.
- **HRV** — if he has a wearable (Whoop, Garmin, Oura), trend it. Don't chase daily numbers.
- **Bodyweight** — same conditions, same time. A 1–2 kg overnight drop usually means dehydration, not progress.

### Red flags for the trainer

These trigger a conversation, not just a logbook entry:
- Sleep <6 hours for 3+ nights in a row
- Resting HR elevated for 5+ days
- Any return of leg symptoms (immediate physio referral)
- Morning back stiffness >30 min lasting beyond a single day
- Subjective energy <5/10 for a week
- Mood drop or irritability persisting beyond a few days

The response is almost always the same: reduce training stress (volume first, then intensity), prioritise sleep, hold for 5–7 days, reassess.

---

## What NOT to Bother With

Worth being explicit about the recovery industry noise:

- **Ice baths** — fine occasionally, but blunting inflammation post-strength training reduces hypertrophy adaptation. Skip them in Phase 2 especially. Cold showers are fine.
- **Massage guns** — pleasant, modest benefit, not worth optimising around
- **Compression boots** — minimal evidence relative to cost
- **Expensive supplements marketed for recovery** — magnesium, creatine, omega-3, and adequate protein cover 95% of what supplementation can offer
- **Sleep tracking obsession** — wearables are useful for trends, harmful when they cause sleep anxiety. If his Oura score is making him anxious, take the ring off.

The hierarchy is, in order: **sleep > food > daily movement > stress management > everything else.** Spend energy on the top of that list.

| Wake | 10 min daylight outside, water |

| Element | Frequency |

| Cardio | 2x/week (Tue LISS, Sat intervals) |

| Rest days | Thursday, Sunday |

| Phase | Weeks | Focus | Main lift rep range | RPE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — Foundation** | 1–4 | Motor control, tissue tolerance, McGill trunk work | 6–10 | 6–7 |
| **2 — Hypertrophy (Push)** | 5–8 | Muscle gain, structural strength, intensity dialled up | 4–8 | 8–8.5 |
| **3 — Strength Peak** | 9–12 | Heavier expression, 1RM test in week 12 | 3–5 | 8–9 |

### Test day protocol summary
- Warm-up: 15–20 min (bike, McGill Big 3, mobility, bodyweight movement, empty bar work)
- Working warm-ups: 40% × 5, 55% × 5, 70% × 3, 80% × 2, 87% × 1
- **Opener:** ~92% (RPE 8)
- **Second:** ~97% (RPE 9)
- **Third (PR attempt):** 100–103%
- Three attempts maximum. Form is the gate. Belt allowed top sets, straps allowed if grip-limited.

## Nutrition Summary (Anti-Inflammatory Framework)

### Core principles
- Protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg/day across 3–4 meals (oily fish 2–3x/week minimum)
- 6–8 portions veg/fruit daily, emphasis on colour and variety
- Prioritise omega-3, EVOO, avocado, nuts; reduce seed oils and ultra-processed foods
- Whole-food carbs (oats, quinoa, sweet potato, sourdough, beans)
- Generous use of turmeric, ginger, garlic, cinnamon
- 2.5–3 L water/day
- Alcohol ≤4 units/week
- 80/20 rule on adherence

### Daily template
- Breakfast: protein + fruit + healthy fat
- Lunch: protein + veg + complex carb + olive oil
- Pre/post-training: protein + carb
- Dinner: protein + 2 veg + complex carb
- Optional evening: light protein

### Supplements
- **Recommended:** Omega-3 (2–3g EPA+DHA), Vitamin D3 (1–2,000 IU), creatine (5g), whey
- **Optional:** Curcumin, collagen pre-training, magnesium glycinate evening
- **Skip:** Multivits, BCAAs, glucosamine, greens powders

### Phase alignment
- Phase 1: establish habits, eat at maintenance
- Phase 2: modest deficit (~200–300 kcal) if fat loss is a goal; high protein
- Phase 3: maintenance or slight surplus — fuel the peak, don't diet through it

## Abs Programming Summary

Trained twice weekly as finishers across four categories: anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral flexion, hip flexion with neutral spine.

- **End of Session A:** anti-rotation + anti-lateral focus

- **Session C:** trunk work already built in (bird dog, side plank, carries)

**Avoid:** crunches, sit-ups, GHD sit-ups, cable crunches, Jefferson curls, weighted Russian twists, V-ups, ab wheel without neutral spine control.

- 10 min daylight within 30 min of waking

- **Sunday:** longer walk, optional sauna, slower spine hygiene, early bed

### Phase adjustments
- Phase 1: install the habits
- Phase 2: 8 hours non-negotiable on training nights, add pre-bed protein
- Phase 3: 2-hour wind-down, zero alcohol from wk 11, extra hour wks 11–12

### Monitoring (low-burden)
Morning 1–10 scores on: sleep quality, energy, soreness, back feel. Resting HR weekly trend.

- Sleep <6 hours for 3+ nights
- Resting HR up >5 bpm for 5+ days
- Any return of leg symptoms → immediate physio referral
- Morning back stiffness >30 min

# 12-Week Strength Programme: Complete Summary

**Client profile:** 42M, desk worker, 8 months post L4-L5 disc herniation, asymptomatic. Physio restrictions: no heavy spinal loading, no loaded spinal flexion. Full gym access.

**Goal:** General strength, body composition improvement, confidence in his body, and a tested 1RM in week 12.

---

## Programme Architecture

| Element | Frequency |
|---|---|
| Strength sessions | 3x/week (Mon/Wed/Fri) |
| Cardio | 2x/week (Tue LISS, Sat intervals) |
| Daily spine hygiene | Every day, 5–10 min |
| Walking | 7,000–10,000 steps/day |
| Abs finishers | 2x/week (end of Sessions A and B) |
| Rest days | Thursday, Sunday |

---

## Phase Overview

| Phase | Weeks | Focus | Main lift rep range | RPE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — Foundation** | 1–4 | Motor control, tissue tolerance, McGill trunk work | 6–10 | 6–7 |
| **2 — Hypertrophy (Push)** | 5–8 | Muscle gain, structural strength, intensity dialled up | 4–8 | 8–8.5 |
| **3 — Strength Peak** | 9–12 | Heavier expression, 1RM test in week 12 | 3–5 | 8–9 |

Deload at week 4 and week 8. Taper week 12.

---

## Weekly Structure

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| **Mon** | Strength A — Lower (hip-dominant) |
| **Tue** | LISS cardio + spine hygiene |
| **Wed** | Strength B — Upper (push/pull) |
| **Thu** | Rest, walking, spine hygiene |
| **Fri** | Strength C — Lower (quad-dominant) / carry |
| **Sat** | Interval cardio + mobility |
| **Sun** | Walking, spine hygiene, recovery anchor day |

---

## PHASE 1 — Foundation & Motor Control (Weeks 1–4)

### Session A — Lower (Hip-Dominant)
- McGill Big 3 (curl-up, side plank, bird dog)
- Trap bar deadlift (high handles) — 4×6 @ RPE 6
- Goblet squat — 3×8
- Single-leg leg press — 3×10/leg
- Seated hamstring curl — 3×12
- Pallof press — 3×10/side
- Dead bug — 2×10/side

### Session B — Upper
- McGill Big 3
- Chest-supported DB row — 4×8
- Half-kneeling landmine press — 3×8/side
- Neutral-grip lat pulldown — 3×10
- Incline DB press — 3×10
- Face pulls — 3×15
- Farmer's carry — 3×30m
- **Abs finisher:** Dead bug 3×8/side + plank 3×30s

### Session C — Full Body / Single-Leg
- Bird dog + side plank
- Rear-foot elevated split squat — 4×8/leg
- Tall-kneeling cable row — 3×10
- 45° back extension (hip hinge only) — 3×12
- Half-kneeling single-arm cable press — 3×10/side
- Suitcase carry — 3×30m/side
- Side plank with reach — 2×8/side

### Phase 1 progression
- Wk 1: prescribed loads, RPE 6
- Wk 2: +5% main lifts, RPE 6–7
- Wk 3: add a set or +5%
- Wk 4: deload — sets reduced 30%

### Phase 1 cardio
- **Tue LISS:** 25→35 min Zone 2 (recumbent bike or incline walk)
- **Sat intervals:** 5→7 rounds of (1 min moderate / 2 min easy)
- Wk 4: skip intervals, easy outdoor walk

---

## PHASE 2 — Hypertrophy & Intensity Push (Weeks 5–8)

### Session A — Lower (Hip-Dominant)
- Bird dog + Pallof press
- Trap bar deadlift — **5×4 @ RPE 8**, top set RPE 8.5 by wk 7
- Barbell hip thrust (paused) — 4×6 @ RPE 8
- **Safety bar squat** (introduced cautiously) — 3×6 @ RPE 7, or heavy goblet/belt squat as sub
- Bulgarian split squat — 4×6/leg, RPE 9 final set
- Lying hamstring curl, 3-sec eccentric — 3×8
- Standing calf raise — 3×10
- Pallof iso-hold — 3×30s/side

### Session B — Upper
- McGill Big 3, abbreviated
- Chest-supported row — 5×5 @ RPE 8
- Incline DB press — 4×6 @ RPE 8
- **Weighted pull-up** (or neutral-grip pulldown) — 4×6 @ RPE 8
- Half-kneeling landmine press — 3×8/side
- DB lateral raise w/ partial dropset — 3×12
- Face pull — 3×15
- EZ-bar curl — 3×8
- Rope triceps pushdown — 3×10
- Heavy farmer's carry — 3×30m
- **Abs finisher:** Hollow hold 3×30s + hanging knee raise 3×8

### Session C — Lower (Quad-Dominant) / Carry
- Side plank + dead bug
- Front-foot elevated reverse lunge — 4×6/leg @ RPE 8
- Leg press — 4×8 @ RPE 8
- RDL with dumbbells — 4×6 @ RPE 8 (cable pull-through sub if form breaks)
- Cable pull-through — 3×10
- Heavy farmer's carry — 4×40m
- Hanging knee raise — 3×10
- Sled push — 4×20m

### Phase 2 progression
- Wk 5: new variations introduced at RPE 7–8
- Wk 6: +5% mains, accessories RPE 8–9
- Wk 7: top set RPE 8.5, add a set to hip thrust + row, AMRAP finals on splits and pull-ups
- Wk 8: deload — volume −40%, intensity RPE 6–7

### Phase 2 cardio
- **Tue LISS:** 35→45 min Zone 2
- **Sat intervals:** dropped to 6 rounds of (1 min hard / 90s easy) to protect recovery
- Wk 8: skip intervals, 40 min easy walk/swim

### Phase 2 nutrition adjustment
- Protein up to 2.0 g/kg/day
- +30–50g carbs on training days
- Narrow any fat-loss deficit to ~200 kcal or shift to maintenance wks 6–7
- Add creatine 5g/day if not already on it
- Pre-bed protein snack on training days

---

## PHASE 3 — Strength Peak & 1RM Test (Weeks 9–12)

### Session A — Lower Strength
- McGill Big 3
- Trap bar deadlift — progression below
- Barbell hip thrust — 4×6 @ RPE 8
- Walking lunge, DBs — 3×8/leg
- Seated leg curl — 3×10
- Pallof iso-hold — 3×30s/side

### Session B — Upper Strength
- Bird dog + side plank
- Chest-supported row — 5×5 @ RPE 8
- Incline DB press — 4×6
- Half-kneeling landmine press — 3×8/side
- Weighted pull-up or pulldown — 3×8
- Rear delt fly — 3×12
- Hammer curl — 3×10
- Heavy farmer's carry — 3×40m
- **Abs finisher:** Ab wheel from knees 3×6 + hanging leg raise 3×8

### Session C — Lower Hybrid / Athletic
- McGill Big 3
- Front-foot elevated split squat — 4×6/leg, heavy DBs
- Single-leg leg press — 3×8/leg
- Cable pull-through — 3×10
- Step-up, DBs — 3×8/leg
- Sled push or carry medley — 4 rounds
- Side plank with leg lift — 3×8/side

### Phase 3 trap bar deadlift progression (build to 1RM)
- **Wk 9:** 5×3 @ RPE 7 — intro, focus on bar speed
- **Wk 10:** 4×3 @ RPE 8 + one heavy single @ RPE 8 (~85%)
- **Wk 11:** work up to heavy single @ RPE 8.5 (~90%) + 2×3 backoff @ 80% — dress rehearsal
- **Wk 12:** taper and **1RM test on Saturday**

### Phase 3 cardio
- **Tue LISS:** 40 min Zone 2 (his choice of modality)
- **Sat intervals:** rotate Option A (bike VO2 5×2/2), Option B (sled medley), Option C (rower 10×250m)
- Wk 11: reduce LISS to 35 min
- Wk 12: 30 min easy Tue, no intervals (Sat is the test)

---

## WEEK 12 — Taper & 1RM Test Day

| Day | Plan |
|---|---|
| Mon | Primer: trap bar single @ RPE 7 (~80%), hip thrust 2×6 @ RPE 6, Pallof iso, out in 35 min |
| Tue | 25 min easy LISS |
| Wed | Upper session, light, RPE 6, ~30 min |
| Thu | Full rest, walking only, no caffeine after noon, in bed by 10:30pm |
| Fri | Complete rest, no alcohol, light dinner with carbs, in bed by 10pm |
| **Sat** | **1RM test — trap bar deadlift** |
| Sun | 30–60 min recovery walk |

### Test day protocol summary
- Warm-up: 15–20 min (bike, McGill Big 3, mobility, bodyweight movement, empty bar work)
- Working warm-ups: 40% × 5, 55% × 5, 70% × 3, 80% × 2, 87% × 1
- **Opener:** ~92% (RPE 8)
- **Second:** ~97% (RPE 9)
- **Third (PR attempt):** 100–103%
- Three attempts maximum. Form is the gate. Belt allowed top sets, straps allowed if grip-limited.
- Stop immediately on any form breakdown or back warning sign.

---

## Daily Spine Hygiene Routine (Every Day, 5–10 min)

- Cat-cow — 8 reps (pain-free range)
- Couch stretch (hip flexor) — 45s/side
- 90/90 hip switches — 8/side
- Glute bridge — 10 reps
- Bird dog — 6/side
- Dead hang — 20–30s × 2

Plus: stand and move every 30 min during the workday.

---

## Nutrition Summary (Anti-Inflammatory Framework)

### Core principles
- Protein 1.6–2.0 g/kg/day across 3–4 meals (oily fish 2–3x/week minimum)
- 6–8 portions veg/fruit daily, emphasis on colour and variety
- Prioritise omega-3, EVOO, avocado, nuts; reduce seed oils and ultra-processed foods
- Whole-food carbs (oats, quinoa, sweet potato, sourdough, beans)
- Generous use of turmeric, ginger, garlic, cinnamon
- 2.5–3 L water/day
- Alcohol ≤4 units/week
- 80/20 rule on adherence

### Daily template
- Breakfast: protein + fruit + healthy fat
- Lunch: protein + veg + complex carb + olive oil
- Pre/post-training: protein + carb
- Dinner: protein + 2 veg + complex carb
- Optional evening: light protein

### Supplements
- **Recommended:** Omega-3 (2–3g EPA+DHA), Vitamin D3 (1–2,000 IU), creatine (5g), whey
- **Optional:** Curcumin, collagen pre-training, magnesium glycinate evening
- **Skip:** Multivits, BCAAs, glucosamine, greens powders

### Phase alignment
- Phase 1: establish habits, eat at maintenance
- Phase 2: modest deficit (~200–300 kcal) if fat loss is a goal; high protein
- Phase 3: maintenance or slight surplus — fuel the peak, don't diet through it

---

## Abs Programming Summary

Trained twice weekly as finishers across four categories: anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral flexion, hip flexion with neutral spine.

- **End of Session A:** anti-rotation + anti-lateral focus
- **End of Session B:** anti-extension + hip flexion focus
- **Session C:** trunk work already built in (bird dog, side plank, carries)

Progression: Phase 1 beginner variations → Phase 2 intermediate → Phase 3 advanced (ab wheel rollout, hanging straight-leg raise, L-sit).

**Avoid:** crunches, sit-ups, GHD sit-ups, cable crunches, Jefferson curls, weighted Russian twists, V-ups, ab wheel without neutral spine control.

---

## Sleep & Recovery Summary

### Sleep
- 7.5–8.5 hours in bed nightly, consistent times (±30 min)
- 90-min wind-down: dim lights, screens away, hot shower, cool dark bedroom
- Phone out of the bedroom
- 10 min daylight within 30 min of waking
- Caffeine cut-off 2pm
- No heavy spinal loading in first 60 min after waking

### Daily recovery
- Stand/move every 30 min at desk
- 2.5–3 L water/day, electrolytes on training days
- Protein at every meal, optional pre-bed protein snack
- 3–5 min slow breathing at lunch and bedtime

### Weekly recovery anchors
- **Thursday:** intentional downshift, easy walk, early bed
- **Saturday afternoon:** 15–20 min mobility session
- **Sunday:** longer walk, optional sauna, slower spine hygiene, early bed

### Phase adjustments
- Phase 1: install the habits
- Phase 2: 8 hours non-negotiable on training nights, add pre-bed protein
- Phase 3: 2-hour wind-down, zero alcohol from wk 11, extra hour wks 11–12

### Monitoring (low-burden)
Morning 1–10 scores on: sleep quality, energy, soreness, back feel. Resting HR weekly trend.

### Red flags (pull back or refer)
- Sleep <6 hours for 3+ nights
- Resting HR up >5 bpm for 5+ days
- Any return of leg symptoms → immediate physio referral
- Morning back stiffness >30 min
- Sharp pain during/after lifting

---

## Contraindications — Locked Across All Phases

- ❌ Back squat, front squat under significant load
- ❌ Conventional barbell deadlift
- ❌ Barbell bent-over row
- ❌ Heavy standing overhead press
- ❌ Sit-ups, crunches, GHD sit-ups, Jefferson curls, cable crunches
- ❌ Good mornings
- ❌ Loaded spinal flexion or rotation in any form
- ❌ Heavy spinal loading within 60 min of waking

---

## Key Milestones to Mark

- **Wk 4:** First deload complete, motor patterns grooved
- **Wk 8:** Hypertrophy block complete, intensity tolerance proven
- **Wk 11:** Heavy single at ~90% — dress rehearsal
- **Wk 12 Sat:** Trap bar deadlift 1RM test
- **Wk 11 submaximal markers:** Chest-supported row 5RM, Bulgarian split squat 6RM/leg, max strict pull-ups, heavy farmer's carry distance

---

## After Week 12

Don't let momentum drop. Plan a brief debrief in the week after the test:
- Log the number, review what worked
- 7–10 days of reduced-volume training (RPE 6–7, 60% volume)
- Decide the next 8-week block — likely hypertrophy-biased given his work capacity will now be there
- Reassess physio status and consider whether to gradually reintroduce variations like safety bar squat at heavier loads, or rack pulls from above the knee
